quiz.q: What's the key difference between an array like `[i32; 3]` and a `Vec<i32>`?
options: Arrays can hold any type, Vec cannot
Vec's length can change at runtime; an array's length is fixed at compile time
Vec is stored on the stack, arrays are always on the heap
There is no real difference
quiz.explain: Vec<T> is a growable, heap-allocated list. An array's size is part of its type and can never change.

options: Vec::new() is faster in every case
Vec::new() starts empty; vec![...] is a macro that builds a Vec already filled with the listed values
vec![...] can only hold strings
They are two names for the exact same function
quiz.explain: Vec::new() gives you an empty vector to push into later; the vec! macro is shorthand for building one pre-populated with known values.

options: The popped value directly, panicking if the vector is empty
Option<T> — Some(value) if there was an element, None if the vector was empty
The new length of the vector
A reference to the popped value that stays valid after popping
quiz.explain: pop() can't return a bare value because the vector might be empty, so it returns an Option — the same 'don't crash, tell the caller' pattern used elsewhere in Rust.

quiz.q: What happens when you evaluate `v[99]` on a vector with only 5 elements?
options: It returns None
It returns a default value like 0
It panics at runtime with 'index out of bounds'
It silently returns garbage memory
quiz.explain: Indexing with [] panics on an out-of-range index rather than reading invalid memory. Use .get(i) if the index might be invalid.

quiz.q: What does `v.get(99)` return if index 99 doesn't exist?
options: It panics, same as v[99]
None — no crash
A reference to the last element instead
It returns 0
quiz.explain: .get(i) returns Option<&T>: Some(&value) if the index is valid, None otherwise — the crash-free alternative to indexing with [].

quiz.q: What's the difference between `for x in &v` and `for x in v`?
options: No difference at all
for x in &v borrows the vector (still usable afterward); for x in v consumes it (v can't be used after the loop)
for x in v is always faster
for x in &v only works with numbers
quiz.explain: &v borrows, yielding &T and leaving the vector intact. Iterating v directly takes ownership and yields owned T, consuming the vector.

quiz.q: Why doesn't `nums.dedup()` remove all duplicates from `vec![1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3]`?
options: dedup() is broken and should never be used
dedup() only removes duplicates that are adjacent to each other, and the two 1-runs aren't adjacent here
dedup() only works on sorted numeric vectors
dedup() requires the elements to implement Copy
quiz.explain: dedup() collapses consecutive equal runs only. To remove all duplicates regardless of position, sort() first so equal elements become neighbors, then dedup().

quiz.q: What's the benefit of `Vec::with_capacity(n)` over `Vec::new()` when you know you'll push exactly n elements?
options: It makes the elements immutable
It reserves space for n elements up front, so those pushes don't trigger any reallocation and copying
It automatically sorts elements as they're pushed
It changes the vector's element type
quiz.explain: Without with_capacity, a growing Vec occasionally has to allocate a bigger block and copy every element over. Reserving the space up front avoids that entirely for known sizes.

options: Removes elements where the closure returns false, keeping only elements where it returns true, in place
Sorts the vector by evenness
Returns a new vector, leaving nums unchanged
Panics if any element is odd
quiz.explain: retain walks the vector and keeps only elements for which the closure returns true, mutating the vector in place.

flashcards.front: Vec::new() vs vec![...] — when to use each?
flashcards.back: Vec::new() for an empty vector you'll fill later with push(); vec![...] when you already know the starting values.

flashcards.front: v[i] vs v.get(i) — what's the difference on an invalid index?
flashcards.back: v[i] panics (crashes) on an out-of-range index. v.get(i) returns None instead — no crash, use it when the index isn't already known to be valid.

flashcards.front: What type does Vec::pop() return, and why?
flashcards.back: Option<T> — Some(value) or None — because the vector might be empty and there'd be nothing to pop.

flashcards.front: for x in &v vs for x in v.
flashcards.back: &v borrows (v stays usable after the loop, x is &T). Plain v consumes ownership (v is gone after, x is owned T).
sort_by takes a closure comparing two full elements and returning Ordering. sort_by_key takes a closure extracting one field to compare by — clearer when sorting by a single field.
Only consecutive (adjacent) equal elements. Sort first if you want every duplicate removed regardless of position.
It reserves room for n elements up front, avoiding the reallocate-and-copy cost that happens when a Vec grows past its current capacity one push at a time.
Keeps only the elements for which the closure f returns true, removing the rest, in place.
